cards.stem: Congress passes a law regulating purely intrastate commercial activity that, in the aggregate, substantially affects interstate commerce. Which doctrine most directly supports Congress's power to enact this law?

choices.text: The Necessary and Proper Clause alone
The aggregate effects doctrine under the Commerce Clause (Wickard v. Filburn)
The 10th Amendment's reservation of state powers
Substantive due process under the 14th Amendment

cards.explanation: Wickard v. Filburn (1942) established that Congress may regulate purely intrastate activity where the AGGREGATE effect of similar activities substantially affects interstate commerce. This survives Lopez/Morrison so long as the regulated activity is ECONOMIC in character; it remains the core post-New Deal Commerce Clause justification.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1 (initial bank). Cites Wickard v. Filburn, 317 U.S. 111 (1942).

cards.stem: Congress enacts a federal statute making it a crime to possess a firearm within 1,000 feet of a public school. The activity regulated is non-commercial. The statute is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under the Commerce Clause because firearms move in interstate commerce
Constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Unconstitutional as exceeding Congress's Commerce Clause power
Constitutional under the Spending Clause

cards.explanation: United States v. Lopez (1995) struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act because gun possession near a school is not economic/commercial activity. Congress's Commerce Clause power reaches (1) channels, (2) instrumentalities, or (3) activities that substantially affect interstate commerce — but Lopez/Morrison (2000) hold that NON-economic intrastate activity cannot be aggregated to satisfy the third category.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites United States v. Lopez, 514 U.S. 549 (1995); United States v. Morrison, 529 U.S. 598 (2000).

cards.stem: A state enacts a tax that applies only to out-of-state vendors selling within the state, while exempting in-state vendors. Without express congressional authorization, the tax is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under the state's police power
Constitutional under the 10th Amendment
Unconstitutional as violating the Dormant Commerce Clause
Constitutional under the Privileges and Immunities Clause

cards.explanation: The Dormant Commerce Clause prohibits state laws that facially discriminate against interstate commerce. Such laws are subject to 'virtually per se invalidity' (City of Philadelphia v. New Jersey) and survive only on a showing of necessity to a legitimate non-economic purpose with no less-discriminatory means available (Maine v. Taylor).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites City of Philadelphia v. New Jersey, 437 U.S. 617 (1978); Maine v. Taylor, 477 U.S. 131 (1986).

citations.label: City of Philadelphia v. New Jersey, 437 U.S. 617 (1978)

cards.stem: Congress enacts a law that, while not directly authorized by any enumerated power, is reasonably adapted to executing one of the enumerated powers. The most precise constitutional basis is:

choices.text: The 10th Amendment
The Necessary and Proper Clause (Art. I § 8 cl. 18)
The Supremacy Clause
The General Welfare Clause

cards.explanation: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) established that Congress's enumerated powers include implied power to adopt any means 'appropriate' and 'plainly adapted' to executing those powers, so long as not prohibited. This is the textual basis of the Necessary and Proper Clause and Marshall's foundational opinion on implied federal powers.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819).

cards.stem: Congress enacts a law requiring state law enforcement officers to perform background checks on firearms purchasers. The most likely defect is:

choices.text: Violation of the Commerce Clause
Violation of the Necessary and Proper Clause
Violation of the 10th Amendment's anti-commandeering principle
Violation of the Supremacy Clause

cards.explanation: Printz v. United States (1997) held that the federal government cannot commandeer state EXECUTIVE officers to enforce federal regulatory programs. New York v. United States (1992) had already held the same for state LEGISLATURES. The 10th Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine bars federal compulsion of state legislative or executive action.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Printz v. United States, 521 U.S. 898 (1997); New York v. United States, 505 U.S. 144 (1992).

citations.label: New York v. United States, 505 U.S. 144 (1992)

cards.stem: A federal statute regulating airlines contains: 'No state may enact any law affecting airline rates, routes, or services.' A state nonetheless passes a consumer-protection statute imposing penalties for airline-fare disclosure violations. The state statute is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under the state's police power
Preempted by express congressional preemption
Constitutional under the Tenth Amendment
Constitutional because it deals with consumer protection

cards.explanation: Express preemption arises when Congress explicitly displaces state law. Morales v. Trans World Airlines (1992) found exactly this preemption clause in the Airline Deregulation Act and held it preempts state laws 'relating to' airline rates, routes, or services. The Supremacy Clause (Art. VI cl. 2) makes valid federal law supreme over conflicting state law.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Morales v. Trans World Airlines, 504 U.S. 374 (1992).

citations.label: Morales v. Trans World Airlines, 504 U.S. 374 (1992)

cards.stem: A state law requires residents-only hiring on state-funded construction projects. A non-resident challenges the law. The most appropriate constitutional basis is:

choices.text: The 14th Amendment Privileges or Immunities Clause
The Article IV § 2 Privileges and Immunities Clause
The Equal Protection Clause
The Dormant Commerce Clause

cards.explanation: Article IV § 2's Privileges and Immunities Clause prohibits states from discriminating against citizens of other states with respect to 'fundamental rights' including the right to pursue a livelihood. The state must show (a) substantial reason for the discrimination AND (b) the discrimination bears a substantial relation to that reason (United Building & Construction Trades v. Camden).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites United Building & Construction Trades Council v. Mayor & Council of Camden, 465 U.S. 208 (1984).

citations.label: United Bldg. & Constr. Trades Council v. Camden, 465 U.S. 208 (1984)

cards.stem: Congress conditions a state's continued receipt of all federal Medicaid funds on the state's adoption of a substantial Medicaid expansion. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, this conditional grant is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under the unlimited federal spending power
Unconstitutional as economic coercion of states
Unconstitutional under the 10th Amendment
Constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause

cards.explanation: NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) held that conditioning ALL existing Medicaid funds on state acceptance of expansion was unconstitutionally coercive — 'a gun to the head' of states. The federal spending power has limits when conditions become so coercive that 'pressure turns into compulsion.' The four Dole conditions still apply (general welfare, unambiguous, related to federal interest, no other constitutional bar) plus the new coercion limit.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites NFIB v. Sebelius, 567 U.S. 519 (2012); South Dakota v. Dole, 483 U.S. 203 (1987).

cards.stem: A private citizen sues a state in federal court for damages alleging a state agency violated federal employment-discrimination law. Absent congressional abrogation under a valid 14A § 5 exercise, the suit is most likely:

choices.text: Permitted under the Supremacy Clause
Barred by state sovereign immunity (11th Amendment)
Permitted because the cause of action arises under federal law
Barred by the Article III case-or-controversy requirement

cards.explanation: The 11th Amendment (and underlying state sovereign immunity) bars private federal-court suits against non-consenting states. Congress can abrogate this immunity ONLY when acting under the 14A § 5 enforcement power AND with a 'clear statement' (Seminole Tribe v. Florida; Kimel v. Florida Bd. of Regents). Article I powers (e.g., Commerce) do NOT support abrogation.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Seminole Tribe v. Florida, 517 U.S. 44 (1996); Kimel v. Florida Bd. of Regents, 528 U.S. 62 (2000).

citations.label: Kimel v. Florida Bd. of Regents, 528 U.S. 62 (2000)

cards.stem: The President negotiates a sole-executive agreement with a foreign nation that affects domestic commerce. The agreement is not submitted to the Senate. Its domestic legal effect within the U.S. depends most directly on:

choices.text: The Treaty Clause's two-thirds Senate requirement
The President's exclusive Article II foreign-affairs power
Whether Congress has authorized executive agreements in the area
The Supremacy Clause alone

cards.explanation: Sole-executive agreements bind the U.S. internationally but their DOMESTIC legal effect typically requires either congressional authorization (Dames & Moore v. Regan) or independent presidential constitutional authority. Under the Youngstown framework (Jackson concurrence), executive action carries the most weight when authorized by Congress (Category 1) and the least when contrary to congressional will (Category 3).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Dames & Moore v. Regan, 453 U.S. 654 (1981); Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952) (Jackson, J., concurring).

citations.label: Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952)

cards.stem: The President issues an executive order seizing private steel mills to ensure war production where Congress has not declared war or authorized presidential seizure. Under the Youngstown framework, the action is in:

choices.text: Category 1 (acting pursuant to congressional authorization)
Category 2 (Congress is silent — twilight zone)
Category 3 (acting against express or implied congressional will) — weakest ground
None of the categories applies

cards.explanation: This is the Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer (1952) fact pattern. Justice Jackson's three-category concurrence is the operative framework. Truman's seizure failed because Congress had implicitly forbidden such action through prior labor-management statutes (Taft-Hartley) — Category 3, where presidential power is at its lowest ebb.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952).

citations.label: Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952)
Patricia L. Bellia, The Story of the Steel Seizure Case (Stanford Law Review)

cards.stem: A federal grand jury subpoenas tape recordings of presidential conversations potentially relevant to a criminal investigation. The President asserts executive privilege as an absolute bar to disclosure. The privilege is:

choices.text: Absolute — communications immune from compelled disclosure
Qualified — must yield to a demonstrated, specific need in a criminal proceeding
Inapplicable to communications with non-cabinet advisors
Coextensive with the Speech and Debate Clause

cards.explanation: United States v. Nixon (1974) held that while executive privilege has a legitimate constitutional basis (separation of powers + need for candid advice), it is QUALIFIED. A generalized privilege claim must yield to a 'demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial.' For matters of military, diplomatic, or sensitive national security, the deference is greater.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites United States v. Nixon, 418 U.S. 683 (1974).

cards.stem: Congress authorizes a federal agency to appoint its own administrative law judges who exercise significant discretionary authority but report to and can be removed by the agency head. Under the Appointments Clause, these judges are most likely:

choices.text: Principal officers requiring Senate confirmation
Inferior officers — Congress may vest their appointment in the agency head
Mere employees not subject to the Appointments Clause
Unconstitutional regardless of how they are appointed

cards.explanation: The Appointments Clause (Art. II § 2) requires presidential nomination + Senate confirmation for PRINCIPAL officers, but allows Congress to vest the appointment of INFERIOR officers in the President alone, the Courts of Law, or Heads of Departments. Inferior officers are those whose work is directed and supervised by a superior (Edmond v. United States; Lucia v. SEC, holding SEC ALJs are inferior officers).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Edmond v. United States, 520 U.S. 651 (1997); Lucia v. SEC, 585 U.S. 237 (2018).

cards.stem: A federal agency is headed by a single director who serves a 5-year term and is removable by the President only 'for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance.' A constitutional challenge is most likely to succeed because:

choices.text: Congress lacks authority to limit presidential removal of any officer
Single-director independent agencies violate Article II's vesting of executive power
Five-year terms exceed Article II limits
The for-cause standard is unconstitutionally vague

cards.explanation: Seila Law v. CFPB (2020) held that a SINGLE-director independent agency with for-cause removal protection violates Article II. The Court distinguished Humphrey's Executor (1935), which permitted for-cause removal of MULTI-MEMBER independent regulatory commissions. The single-director structure plus removal protection concentrates executive power outside presidential control.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Seila Law LLC v. CFPB, 591 U.S. 197 (2020); Humphrey's Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935).

citations.label: Seila Law LLC v. CFPB, 591 U.S. 197 (2020)
Humphrey's Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935)

cards.stem: The President issues a pardon for a federal offense. The pardon's scope is:

choices.text: Co-extensive with all federal AND state criminal liability
Limited to federal offenses; state liability is unaffected
Limited to past offenses for which a conviction has been entered
Subject to Senate ratification within 30 days

cards.explanation: The Article II pardon power is plenary but extends only to OFFENSES AGAINST THE UNITED STATES (i.e., federal crimes). It does not reach state criminal liability or civil claims. Pardons may be granted before conviction (Ex parte Garland) and even prospectively to a class (Burdick v. United States), but state-law liability remains.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Ex parte Garland, 71 U.S. (4 Wall.) 333 (1866); Burdick v. United States, 236 U.S. 79 (1915).

cards.stem: The Senate ratifies a treaty by two-thirds vote. Implementing legislation regulates conduct that, absent the treaty, would arguably exceed Congress's Article I powers. The implementing legislation is:

choices.text: Unconstitutional because Congress can only legislate within Article I powers
Constitutional if rationally related to executing the treaty
Always unconstitutional under the 10th Amendment
Constitutional only if the underlying treaty is self-executing

cards.explanation: Missouri v. Holland (1920) held that the Necessary and Proper Clause empowers Congress to enact legislation to execute treaties, even where such legislation might exceed Article I powers absent the treaty. Bond v. United States (2014) narrowed APPLICATION via the federalism canon (reading the Chemical Weapons statute not to reach purely local conduct), but did NOT overrule Holland's broader rule.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Missouri v. Holland, 252 U.S. 416 (1920); Bond v. United States, 572 U.S. 844 (2014).

cards.stem: The President makes appointments without Senate confirmation during a 3-day Senate recess. Under recent Supreme Court doctrine, the appointments are:

choices.text: Constitutional under the Recess Appointments Clause
Unconstitutional because the recess is too short to qualify
Constitutional only if the appointments are of inferior officers
Always constitutional during any Senate adjournment

cards.explanation: NLRB v. Noel Canning (2014) held that for the Recess Appointments Clause to apply, the recess must be of 'sufficient length' — at least 10 days as a presumptive minimum. Three days is presumptively too short. The Court also held the clause applies to both inter-session and substantial intra-session recesses.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites NLRB v. Noel Canning, 573 U.S. 513 (2014).

cards.stem: A former President is criminally indicted in federal court for actions taken while in office. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the former President enjoys:
cards.grammar_point: Presidential immunity — Trump v. United States (2024)

choices.text: No criminal immunity for any acts during the presidency
Absolute immunity for core constitutional powers AND at least presumptive immunity for other official acts
Absolute immunity from all civil and criminal liability
Immunity only for actions involving foreign affairs

cards.explanation: Trump v. United States (2024) established a tiered immunity framework: (1) ABSOLUTE immunity for actions within the President's exclusive constitutional authority (e.g., pardon power, conduct involving DOJ); (2) at least PRESUMPTIVE immunity for other official acts (rebuttable only on a showing that prosecution would not pose dangers to executive functions); (3) NO immunity for unofficial acts.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Trump v. United States, 603 U.S. 593 (2024).

citations.label: Saikrishna B. Prakash, The Sweep and Force of Section Three (U. Pa. L. Rev.)

cards.stem: A federal agency interprets an ambiguous provision of its enabling statute. A regulated party challenges the interpretation in court. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the court should:

choices.text: Defer to the agency's reasonable interpretation under Chevron
Exercise independent judgment to determine the best statutory reading
Defer only if the agency's interpretation is 'permissible'
Defer under Skidmore in all cases regardless of statutory ambiguity

cards.explanation: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) overruled Chevron v. NRDC (1984). Courts must now exercise INDEPENDENT JUDGMENT to determine the best reading of statutory text. Agencies receive only the persuasive weight contemplated by Skidmore v. Swift (1944) — based on the agency's reasoning, expertise, and consistency.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024); Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U.S. 134 (1944).

citations.label: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)

cards.stem: The President orders military action abroad without an explicit declaration of war by Congress. The action lasts months without specific authorization. The most likely judicial analysis is:

choices.text: Per se unconstitutional because only Congress can declare war
Non-justiciable as a political question even if reachable on the merits
Always constitutional under the President's Commander-in-Chief power
Constitutional only with U.N. Security Council approval

cards.explanation: While Article I § 8 grants Congress the power to 'declare war,' federal courts have generally refused to decide war-powers disputes on POLITICAL QUESTION grounds — textually demonstrable commitment to political branches and lack of judicially manageable standards. The War Powers Resolution (1973) imposes statutory limits, but standing/political-question hurdles have caused most challenges (e.g., Campbell v. Clinton) to be dismissed.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Campbell v. Clinton, 203 F.3d 19 (D.C. Cir. 2000); Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186 (1962) (political question test).

cards.stem: A city ordinance bans 'all signs containing political speech' within 100 feet of polling places on election day. The proper level of scrutiny is:

choices.text: Rational basis review
Intermediate scrutiny
Strict scrutiny because the law is content-based
The ordinance is exempt from First Amendment scrutiny

cards.explanation: Content-based speech restrictions — those that 'draw distinctions based on the message a speaker conveys' — receive STRICT SCRUTINY (narrowly tailored to a compelling interest). Reed v. Town of Gilbert (2015) reaffirmed that content discrimination is judged by the law's text, regardless of the government's motive. Singling out 'political speech' is content-based on its face.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 576 U.S. 155 (2015).

citations.label: Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 576 U.S. 155 (2015)

cards.stem: A city ordinance prohibits amplified sound after 10 p.m. in residential neighborhoods. It is content-neutral. The ordinance is most likely:

choices.text: Subject to strict scrutiny because it restricts speech
Constitutional if narrowly tailored to a significant government interest and leaves open alternative channels
Constitutional under any reasonable basis
Per se unconstitutional as a prior restraint

cards.explanation: Content-neutral time/place/manner regulations face INTERMEDIATE SCRUTINY: (1) narrowly tailored, (2) significant government interest, (3) ample alternative channels (Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 1989). Noise-control ordinances are classic examples that survive this test — the interest in residential quiet is significant and alternative channels (daytime amplification, written materials) exist.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989).

citations.label: Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989)

cards.stem: A federal statute prohibits burning draft cards. A defendant burns his card to protest the war and raises a First Amendment defense. Under O'Brien, the statute is upheld if:

choices.text: It serves any conceivable government interest
Its restriction on speech is no greater than essential to further an important and substantial government interest unrelated to suppression of expression
The defendant lacked the intent to communicate
The activity is not symbolic speech

cards.explanation: United States v. O'Brien (1968) controls regulation of conduct with both speech and non-speech elements. Four-part test: (1) within constitutional power; (2) furthers an IMPORTANT or SUBSTANTIAL government interest; (3) the interest is UNRELATED to the suppression of free expression; (4) the incidental restriction on speech is no greater than essential. The Selective Service registration interest sustained the statute.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites United States v. O'Brien, 391 U.S. 367 (1968).

cards.stem: A city park is a traditional public forum. A speaker requests a permit; the city denies based on objections to the speaker's viewpoint. The denial is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under the city's discretion to allocate public space
Unconstitutional as viewpoint-based discrimination in a public forum
Constitutional if the city offers an alternative location
Subject to rational basis review

cards.explanation: In TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUMS (parks, sidewalks, streets), content-based restrictions face strict scrutiny and VIEWPOINT-based discrimination is per se unconstitutional. The government may impose only content-neutral, narrowly tailored time/place/manner regulations (Perry Education Ass'n, 1983). Viewpoint discrimination is the gravest First Amendment violation.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Perry Education Ass'n v. Perry Local Educators' Ass'n, 460 U.S. 37 (1983).

citations.label: Perry Education Ass'n v. Perry Local Educators' Ass'n, 460 U.S. 37 (1983)

cards.stem: A public school football coach engages in personal silent prayer at the 50-yard line after games. The school district disciplines him. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the proper Establishment Clause framework focuses on:

choices.text: The Lemon test's three prongs
Whether the practice is consistent with historical American practices and understandings
Whether the practice has a primary effect of advancing religion
Whether the activity creates excessive government entanglement

cards.explanation: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022) effectively abandoned the Lemon test in favor of an HISTORY-AND-TRADITION analysis. Establishment Clause inquiries now focus on whether the practice is consistent with historical American practices and understandings. The coach's personal prayer was protected; the Court rejected the school district's Establishment Clause concerns as not grounded in historical practice.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022).

citations.label: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022)

cards.stem: A neutral, generally applicable state law incidentally burdens a religious practice. Per current Supreme Court doctrine (and absent a system of individualized exemptions), the law is most likely:
cards.grammar_point: Free Exercise — Employment Division v. Smith

choices.text: Subject to strict scrutiny because it burdens religion
Constitutional under rational basis review
Per se unconstitutional under the Free Exercise Clause
Subject to intermediate scrutiny

cards.explanation: Employment Division v. Smith (1990) held that NEUTRAL, GENERALLY APPLICABLE laws are not subject to strict scrutiny merely because they incidentally burden religion. However, if a law is NOT neutral or NOT generally applicable (Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye v. Hialeah, 1993), or contains a system of individualized exemptions (Fulton v. Philadelphia, 2021), strict scrutiny applies.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Employment Division v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990); Fulton v. Philadelphia, 593 U.S. 522 (2021).

citations.label: Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, 593 U.S. 522 (2021)
Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye v. Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993)

cards.stem: The federal government seeks an injunction to prevent publication of classified national-security documents by a major newspaper. To obtain the injunction, the government must show:

choices.text: The publication would violate any federal statute
The publication would cause direct, immediate, and irreparable damage to the nation
The publication is not in the public interest
The newspaper obtained the documents illegally

cards.explanation: New York Times v. United States (1971) (Pentagon Papers) established that prior restraints on the press carry a 'heavy presumption against constitutional validity.' The government bears a heavy burden to show publication would cause 'direct, immediate, and irreparable' harm. Mere national-security embarrassment or general harm to relations is insufficient.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites New York Times Co. v. United States, 403 U.S. 713 (1971).

citations.label: New York Times Co. v. United States, 403 U.S. 713 (1971)

cards.stem: A state regulation restricts truthful, non-misleading advertising of a lawful product. Under Central Hudson, the regulation is constitutional if:

choices.text: It serves any conceivable government interest
It directly advances a substantial government interest and is no more extensive than necessary
It is content-neutral
It is narrowly tailored to a compelling interest

cards.explanation: Central Hudson Gas & Electric v. PSC (1980) provides intermediate-scrutiny review for commercial speech. Four-part test: (1) speech is truthful and lawful, (2) substantial government interest, (3) regulation directly advances that interest, (4) regulation is no more extensive than necessary. Truthful, non-misleading ads of lawful products receive significant protection.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Commission, 447 U.S. 557 (1980).

citations.label: Central Hudson Gas & Elec. Corp. v. Public Serv. Comm'n, 447 U.S. 557 (1980)

cards.stem: A state university maintains an admissions policy that uses race as one factor in admissions decisions. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the policy is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under intermediate scrutiny
Unconstitutional as a violation of the Equal Protection Clause
Constitutional under rational basis review
Constitutional if narrowly tailored to a compelling interest

cards.explanation: Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) effectively ended race-conscious admissions in higher education, holding that Harvard's and UNC's race-conscious admissions programs violated the Equal Protection Clause. The diversity rationale (Grutter v. Bollinger, 2003) was insufficient to satisfy strict scrutiny. Race-based government classifications still face strict scrutiny, but admissions policies fail it.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Students for Fair Admissions v. President & Fellows of Harvard College, 600 U.S. 181 (2023).

citations.label: Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181 (2023)

cards.stem: A state law differentiates between men and women in providing certain benefits. The classification is reviewed under:

choices.text: Strict scrutiny
Intermediate scrutiny — substantially related to an important government interest
Rational basis review
Heightened rational basis review

cards.explanation: Craig v. Boren (1976) established INTERMEDIATE SCRUTINY for gender classifications: substantially related to an important government interest. United States v. Virginia (1996) (VMI) refined this with an 'exceedingly persuasive justification' requirement, but the test remains intermediate, not strict.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Craig v. Boren, 429 U.S. 190 (1976); United States v. Virginia, 518 U.S. 515 (1996).

cards.stem: A state law treats different categories of business owners differently for tax purposes. The classification implicates no suspect class or fundamental right. The proper level of scrutiny is:

choices.text: Strict scrutiny
Intermediate scrutiny
Rational basis review
The classification is per se unconstitutional

cards.explanation: Economic and social classifications that don't implicate suspect classes or fundamental rights receive RATIONAL BASIS review — the law must be rationally related to a legitimate interest. The standard is highly deferential; courts uphold unless the classification is 'wholly irrelevant' to a legitimate purpose.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Allied Stores of Ohio v. Bowers, 358 U.S. 522 (1959); FCC v. Beach Communications, 508 U.S. 307 (1993).

citations.label: Allied Stores of Ohio v. Bowers, 358 U.S. 522 (1959)

cards.stem: A state law substantially burdens the right to marry. The most appropriate analytical framework is:

choices.text: Strict scrutiny because marriage is a fundamental right
Rational basis because no fundamental right is implicated
Intermediate scrutiny
Per se constitutional

cards.explanation: Marriage is a fundamental right protected by substantive due process (Loving v. Virginia, 1967; Obergefell v. Hodges, 2015). Substantial restrictions on the right to marry must satisfy strict scrutiny. Reasonable regulations (e.g., minimum age, blood tests, license fees) that don't UNDULY burden the right typically survive even heightened review.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1 (1967); Obergefell v. Hodges, 576 U.S. 644 (2015).

cards.stem: A state agency terminates a recipient's welfare benefits based on a paperwork review without prior hearing. The court applies the Mathews v. Eldridge balancing test, weighing:

choices.text: The financial cost of additional process versus government efficiency
The private interest, the risk of erroneous deprivation, and the government's interest
Only the government's interest in efficient administration
Only whether the deprivation was substantial

cards.explanation: Mathews v. Eldridge (1976) three-factor balancing: (1) PRIVATE INTEREST affected, (2) RISK OF ERRONEOUS DEPRIVATION through current procedures and the value of additional safeguards, (3) GOVERNMENT'S INTEREST including the burden of additional procedures. Welfare termination requires a pre-termination hearing (Goldberg v. Kelly, 1970); Social Security disability terminations don't (Mathews itself).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976); Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970).

cards.stem: A private shopping mall prohibits political leafleting on its premises. A leafleter sues alleging First Amendment violation. The most likely outcome:

choices.text: The leafleter wins because shopping malls are public forums
The mall wins because no state action is involved
The leafleter wins under the 'company town' exception
The case must be analyzed under the Equal Protection Clause

cards.explanation: Constitutional rights generally apply only against STATE action, not private action. A private shopping mall, even if open to the public, is not state action (Hudgens v. NLRB, 1976; Lloyd Corp. v. Tanner, 1972). The 'company town' exception (Marsh v. Alabama, 1946) is narrow — the entity must perform functions traditionally and EXCLUSIVELY reserved to the state.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Hudgens v. NLRB, 424 U.S. 507 (1976); Marsh v. Alabama, 326 U.S. 501 (1946).

cards.stem: A state enacts a law restricting abortion. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the law most likely is reviewed under:

choices.text: Strict scrutiny because abortion is a fundamental right under Roe v. Wade
Rational basis review
Intermediate scrutiny
The undue burden standard from Planned Parenthood v. Casey

cards.explanation: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022) overruled Roe v. Wade (1973) and Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), holding that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion. State abortion regulations are now reviewed under RATIONAL BASIS, with abortion regulation returned primarily to state democratic processes.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, 597 U.S. 215 (2022).

citations.label: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Org., 597 U.S. 215 (2022)

cards.stem: A state requires a license to carry a concealed firearm in public, conditioned on demonstrating 'proper cause' (a specific need exceeding general self-defense). Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the requirement is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under intermediate scrutiny
Unconstitutional under the Second Amendment
Constitutional under rational basis review
Constitutional under the police-power doctrine

cards.explanation: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen (2022) held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to carry firearms in public for self-defense. Gun regulations must be consistent with the 'historical tradition of firearm regulation.' 'May-issue' or 'proper cause' regimes giving officials discretion to deny permits to law-abiding citizens were struck down.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022).

citations.label: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)
District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)

cards.stem: Police, without a warrant, attach a GPS tracker to a suspect's car parked on public streets, monitoring its location for a month. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the action constitutes:

choices.text: A non-search because the suspect was on public streets
A search requiring a warrant under the Fourth Amendment
A search constitutional under the Carroll automobile exception
A search constitutional because no physical intrusion occurred

cards.explanation: United States v. Jones (2012) held that physically attaching a GPS tracker to a vehicle is a 'search' because it constitutes physical trespass on a constitutionally protected area (Katz reasonable-expectation-of-privacy + Jones property-based test). Carpenter v. United States (2018) extended the warrant requirement to long-term cellphone location data — long-term comprehensive tracking is a search regardless of physical intrusion.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites United States v. Jones, 565 U.S. 400 (2012); Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296 (2018).

cards.stem: Police lawfully arrest a suspect in his home and search the area within his immediate control (his 'wingspan'). The search is:

choices.text: Unconstitutional because no warrant was obtained
Constitutional as a search incident to arrest
Unconstitutional because no exigent circumstances exist
Constitutional only with probable cause for the search itself

cards.explanation: Chimel v. California (1969) permits a warrantless search incident to a lawful arrest to (1) preserve evidence and (2) protect officer safety. Scope is limited to the arrestee's PERSON and the area within immediate control ('wingspan'). Riley v. California (2014) carved out cellphones — those generally require a warrant despite being on the arrestee's person.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Chimel v. California, 395 U.S. 752 (1969); Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014).

cards.stem: Police place a suspect in custody for questioning and begin interrogation without giving Miranda warnings. The suspect makes incriminating statements. The statements are most likely:

choices.text: Admissible if voluntary
Inadmissible under Miranda v. Arizona
Admissible if the suspect was given the warnings later
Admissible if the police acted in good faith

cards.explanation: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) requires that suspects in CUSTODY who are subject to INTERROGATION be informed of their rights (silence, counsel, etc.) before questioning. Statements made during un-Mirandized custodial interrogation are presumed involuntary and inadmissible in the prosecution's case-in-chief (though sometimes usable for impeachment per Harris v. New York).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966).

cards.stem: A defendant is acquitted of bank robbery in state court. The federal government then prosecutes the same defendant for federal bank robbery arising from the same incident. The second prosecution is:

choices.text: Barred by the Double Jeopardy Clause
Permitted under the dual sovereignty doctrine
Permitted only with the defendant's consent
Barred unless the federal interest is 'substantial'

cards.explanation: The Dual Sovereignty doctrine permits successive prosecutions by separate sovereigns (state and federal governments) for the same conduct, even after acquittal in one. Gamble v. United States (2019) reaffirmed this principle. State and federal governments are separate sovereigns, each with its own interest in prosecuting offenses against its own laws.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Gamble v. United States, 587 U.S. 678 (2019).

cards.stem: At trial, the prosecution offers the recorded statement of an unavailable witness. The statement is testimonial (made to police during a formal investigation). The defendant had no prior opportunity to cross-examine. The statement is:

choices.text: Admissible under the residual hearsay exception
Inadmissible under the Confrontation Clause
Admissible if the witness is unavailable for valid reason
Admissible if the statement bears 'particularized guarantees of trustworthiness'

cards.explanation: Crawford v. Washington (2004) overruled the Ohio v. Roberts (1980) 'indicia of reliability' framework. The Confrontation Clause bars admission of TESTIMONIAL out-of-court statements unless (1) the declarant is unavailable AND (2) the defendant had a PRIOR OPPORTUNITY to cross-examine. Both must be met. Statements to police during investigation are typically testimonial.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36 (2004).

cards.stem: A defendant is charged with a felony in state court. He is indigent and requests appointed counsel; the state refuses, citing budget constraints. The refusal is:

choices.text: Constitutional because the right to counsel applies only in federal court
Unconstitutional under the Sixth Amendment as incorporated by the Fourteenth
Constitutional if the offense carries no possibility of imprisonment
Constitutional unless the defendant demonstrates likely innocence

cards.explanation: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies in state felony prosecutions through incorporation into the 14A Due Process Clause. The state must provide appointed counsel to indigent defendants in any case where IMPRISONMENT is a possible penalty (extended to misdemeanors with imprisonment in Argersinger v. Hamlin, 1972).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963); Argersinger v. Hamlin, 407 U.S. 25 (1972).

cards.stem: A state imposes the death penalty for a crime not involving the death of a victim. The Supreme Court would most likely find this:

choices.text: Constitutional because the state has substantial deterrence interests
Unconstitutional as disproportionate punishment under the Eighth Amendment
Constitutional under traditional capital punishment doctrine
Constitutional only with bifurcated jury procedures

cards.explanation: The Eighth Amendment prohibits the death penalty for non-homicide crimes against individuals. Coker v. Georgia (1977) struck down the death penalty for the rape of an adult; Kennedy v. Louisiana (2008) struck down capital child rape. The Court applies 'evolving standards of decency' to determine proportionality.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Coker v. Georgia, 433 U.S. 584 (1977); Kennedy v. Louisiana, 554 U.S. 407 (2008).

cards.stem: Police obtain a search warrant based on a sworn affidavit. The warrant is later determined to be technically defective due to a magistrate's error. Evidence obtained from the search is offered at trial. Under the good faith exception:

choices.text: Inadmissible because the warrant was defective
Admissible because police acted in objective good faith reliance on the warrant
Inadmissible regardless of police belief
Admissible only if the defendant fails to object at trial

cards.explanation: United States v. Leon (1984) established the GOOD FAITH EXCEPTION to the exclusionary rule. Evidence obtained pursuant to a search warrant is admissible if executing officers act in OBJECTIVELY REASONABLE RELIANCE on the warrant, even if later found defective. The exclusionary rule's purpose (deterring police misconduct) is not served by suppression when police acted appropriately.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites United States v. Leon, 468 U.S. 897 (1984).

cards.stem: A plaintiff brings suit alleging a federal agency action violates federal environmental law. To establish Article III standing, the plaintiff must show:

choices.text: A reasonable likelihood of success on the merits
Injury in fact, causation, and redressability
Diversity of citizenship between the parties
That the matter involves a 'case of federal interest'

cards.explanation: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992) articulated the three 'irreducible constitutional minimum' elements: (1) INJURY IN FACT (concrete, particularized, actual or imminent); (2) CAUSATION (fairly traceable to challenged action); (3) REDRESSABILITY (likely to be redressed by favorable decision). All three must be shown for federal-court jurisdiction.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992).

citations.label: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
UT Review of Litigation — standing scholarship

cards.stem: A pregnant plaintiff challenges a state law restricting access to abortion. The case takes years to litigate, and the plaintiff is no longer pregnant. Under the mootness doctrine:
cards.grammar_point: Mootness — capable of repetition yet evading review

choices.text: The case is moot because the plaintiff no longer has a personal stake
The case is not moot under the 'capable of repetition yet evading review' exception
The case is moot because the plaintiff lacks standing
The case must be dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction

cards.explanation: A case is normally moot when there's no longer a live controversy. The CAPABLE OF REPETITION YET EVADING REVIEW exception applies when (1) the duration of the action is too short to be fully litigated AND (2) there's a reasonable expectation the same complainant will be subjected to the same action again (Roe v. Wade applied this exception to pregnancy-related litigation).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 113, 125 (1973) (mootness exception application).

cards.stem: A regulated company challenges a federal regulation before the regulation has been applied to its specific case. The agency has not initiated any enforcement action. The challenge is most likely:

choices.text: Justiciable under the present-controversy doctrine
Not ripe for adjudication; the controversy is too abstract
Justiciable under the declaratory judgment principle
Premature only if the agency has not yet adopted the regulation

cards.explanation: Ripeness requires that the controversy be CONCRETE and not hypothetical. Pre-enforcement challenges generally require: (1) hardship to the parties from withholding judicial review AND (2) fitness of the issues for judicial decision (Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner, 1967). A regulation that hasn't been applied may be too abstract to adjudicate without further factual development.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner, 387 U.S. 136 (1967).

citations.label: Susan B. Anthony List v. Driehaus, 573 U.S. 149 (2014)

cards.stem: A senator challenges the constitutional adequacy of impeachment proceedings against him in the U.S. Senate. The case is most likely:
cards.grammar_point: Political question doctrine — Nixon v. United States

choices.text: Justiciable as a routine constitutional question
Non-justiciable as a political question committed to the Senate
Justiciable under the case-or-controversy requirement
Justiciable if the Senate's procedures violate the Constitution

cards.explanation: Nixon v. United States (1993) (federal judge Walter Nixon's impeachment trial) held that challenges to Senate impeachment procedures present a NON-JUSTICIABLE POLITICAL QUESTION. The Constitution gives the Senate 'the sole Power to try all Impeachments.' Textual commitment to a coordinate branch + lack of judicially manageable standards → non-justiciable per Baker v. Carr's six-factor test.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Nixon v. United States, 506 U.S. 224 (1993); Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186 (1962).

cards.stem: A federal taxpayer challenges a federal expenditure that allegedly violates the Establishment Clause. Under Flast v. Cohen and recent Supreme Court doctrine, the taxpayer's standing:

choices.text: Is precluded under the general taxpayer-standing rule
May exist if the challenge is to a congressional taxing-or-spending exercise that violates a specific constitutional limit on that power
Always exists for any constitutional challenge
Exists only if the taxpayer can show a unique personal injury

cards.explanation: Frothingham v. Mellon (1923) generally bars taxpayer standing as a 'generalized grievance.' Flast v. Cohen (1968) carved a NARROW exception for Establishment Clause challenges to CONGRESSIONAL exercises of the taxing/spending power. Hein v. Freedom From Religion Foundation (2007) and Arizona Christian School Tuition Org. v. Winn (2011) substantially narrowed Flast — executive expenditures and tax credits don't qualify.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Flast v. Cohen, 392 U.S. 83 (1968); Hein v. Freedom From Religion Foundation, 551 U.S. 587 (2007).

citations.label: Hein v. Freedom From Religion Foundation, 551 U.S. 587 (2007)

cards.stem: A plaintiff sues alleging that a federal program violates the Constitution but cannot show any concrete personal injury beyond shared concerns with all citizens. The plaintiff most likely:

choices.text: Has standing because constitutional violations affect all citizens
Lacks standing because the injury is a generalized grievance
Has standing as a private attorney general
Has standing if the issue is sufficiently important

cards.explanation: Allen v. Wright (1984) and Lujan held that a 'generalized grievance' — an injury suffered by all citizens equally and indistinguishably — does not satisfy Article III standing's PARTICULARIZED INJURY requirement. The plaintiff must show injury that is concrete, particularized, and 'personal and individual.' Mere interest in proper governance is insufficient absent a concrete personal stake.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #1. Cites Allen v. Wright, 468 U.S. 737 (1984); Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992).

citations.label: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

cards.stem: Congress enacts a federal statute prohibiting states from authorizing sports gambling. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the statute is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under the Commerce Clause
Unconstitutional as commandeering state legislatures
Constitutional under the Spending Clause
Constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause

cards.explanation: Murphy v. NCAA (2018) struck down PASPA's anti-authorization provision as commandeering — Congress cannot directly prohibit state legislatures from acting in their legislative capacity. The 10A anti-commandeering principle from New York v. United States and Printz v. United States extends to legislative-action-prohibition, not just affirmative commandeering.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: New York v. United States, 505 U.S. 144 (1992)

cards.stem: A state requires out-of-state online retailers with no physical presence in the state to collect and remit sales tax. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, this requirement is:

choices.text: Unconstitutional under the physical-presence rule of Quill
Constitutional if the retailer has substantial economic nexus with the state
Constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Unconstitutional as a Dormant Commerce Clause violation per se

cards.explanation: South Dakota v. Wayfair (2018) overruled Quill Corp. v. North Dakota (1992) and held that the Dormant Commerce Clause's substantial-nexus requirement is satisfied by economic and virtual contacts; physical presence is no longer required. States can require out-of-state online sellers to collect sales tax based on substantial economic activity in the state.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: South Dakota v. Wayfair, Inc., 585 U.S. 162 (2018)
Quill Corp. v. North Dakota, 504 U.S. 298 (1992)

cards.stem: A state law prohibits direct-to-consumer wine shipments by out-of-state wineries while permitting in-state wineries to do so. The Twenty-First Amendment is invoked as a defense. The law is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional because the 21A overrides the Dormant Commerce Clause
Unconstitutional because the 21A does not authorize discrimination against out-of-state interests
Constitutional under state police power
Subject to rational basis review only

cards.explanation: Granholm v. Heald (2005) held that the 21A does not save state laws that facially discriminate against out-of-state alcohol producers in favor of in-state producers. Tennessee Wine & Spirits v. Thomas (2019) confirmed and extended this principle to retailers. The 21A's grant of state authority over alcohol does not authorize protectionist discrimination forbidden by the Dormant Commerce Clause.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Tennessee Wine & Spirits Retailers Ass'n v. Thomas, 588 U.S. 504 (2019)

cards.stem: Federal OSHA promulgates a rule requiring covered employers to mandate that employees be vaccinated or undergo regular testing. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the rule is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under OSHA's broad workplace-safety authority
Constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Unconstitutional under the major questions doctrine
Unconstitutional as commandeering employers

cards.explanation: NFIB v. OSHA (2022) (per curiam) stayed OSHA's vaccine-or-test mandate, applying the major questions doctrine: where an agency claims authority to make decisions of vast economic and political significance, Congress must speak clearly. OSHA's enabling statute did not clearly authorize regulating broadly-spread public-health risks like COVID transmission across all workplaces.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

cards.stem: EPA promulgates a rule requiring electricity generators to shift from coal to lower-emission sources, transforming the national power grid. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the rule is most likely:

choices.text: Constitutional under the Clean Air Act's broad delegation
Unconstitutional under the major questions doctrine, requiring clear congressional authorization
Constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Unconstitutional as commandeering states

cards.explanation: West Virginia v. EPA (2022) struck down EPA's Clean Power Plan under the major questions doctrine. The Court held that EPA's claim to authority over generation-shifting was a transformational regulatory decision of major economic and political significance, requiring clear congressional authorization that the Clean Air Act did not provide.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Texas Law Review — major questions doctrine scholarship

cards.stem: A state prosecutes a defendant under a state immigration-related identity-theft statute, where the conduct relates to federally-regulated immigration matters. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the prosecution is most likely:

choices.text: Preempted by federal immigration law
Not preempted because the state law addresses identity-theft conduct, not immigration status
Preempted under the foreign-affairs power
Constitutional under the dormant Commerce Clause

cards.explanation: Kansas v. Garcia (2020) held that federal immigration law (IRCA) does not preempt state identity-theft prosecutions arising from use of false documents to obtain employment, even where the documents related to federally-regulated I-9 processes. State prosecutions of identity theft under generally-applicable state law are not preempted because they regulate conduct beyond the scope of federal immigration law.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

cards.stem: A state enacts a comprehensive immigration enforcement scheme that authorizes state officers to detain individuals based on suspected immigration violations. Per Supreme Court doctrine, the most likely outcome is:

choices.text: Constitutional as concurrent state-federal jurisdiction
Substantial portions are preempted by federal immigration law
Constitutional under the 10th Amendment
Subject to strict scrutiny

cards.explanation: Arizona v. United States (2012) held substantial portions of Arizona's SB 1070 preempted by federal immigration law. The federal government has broad authority over immigration enforcement, and state laws that conflict with or impede federal enforcement priorities are preempted. State officers' authority to detain based on suspected immigration violations is generally preempted absent specific federal authorization.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Chamber of Commerce v. Whiting, 563 U.S. 582 (2011)

cards.stem: A state's congressional district map dilutes Black voting strength in violation of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Per recent Supreme Court doctrine, the appropriate analysis under Section 2 is:

choices.text: Strict scrutiny, requiring narrow tailoring to a compelling interest
The Gingles three-part test for vote dilution claims
Rational basis review
Intermediate scrutiny

cards.explanation: Allen v. Milligan (2023) reaffirmed the Thornburg v. Gingles (1986) three-part framework for Section 2 vote-dilution claims: (1) the minority group is sufficiently large and geographically compact to constitute a majority in a single-member district; (2) the minority group is politically cohesive; (3) the white majority votes sufficiently as a bloc to defeat the minority's preferred candidate. Allen confirmed Section 2's continued vitality.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

cards.stem: A federal court sitting in diversity hears a state-law tort claim. Per the Erie doctrine, the court must apply:

choices.text: Federal common law in all circumstances
State substantive law and federal procedural law
Federal law because the case is in federal court
State law in all respects

cards.explanation: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938) overruled Swift v. Tyson and held there is no federal general common law. Federal courts sitting in diversity must apply state SUBSTANTIVE law to avoid forum-shopping (Hanna v. Plumer outcome-determinative test) but may apply federal procedural law where authorized by the Rules of Decision Act and Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938)

cards.stem: A plaintiff seeks federal-court injunction against a pending state criminal prosecution, alleging the state criminal statute is unconstitutional. Absent extraordinary circumstances, the federal court should:

choices.text: Issue the injunction to vindicate constitutional rights
Abstain under Younger v. Harris
Apply Pullman abstention
Apply Burford abstention

cards.explanation: Younger v. Harris (1971) established that federal courts should generally abstain from enjoining ongoing state criminal prosecutions absent extraordinary circumstances (bad faith, harassment, or patently unconstitutional state statute). The doctrine reflects principles of federalism and comity, allowing state courts the first opportunity to address constitutional challenges to state laws.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: UT Review of Litigation — Younger abstention

cards.stem: A federal-question case requires interpretation of an unclear state statute that, if construed in a particular way, might avoid a federal constitutional question. The federal court should:

choices.text: Decide the federal constitutional question immediately
Abstain under Pullman to allow state-court resolution of the state-law question
Dismiss for lack of jurisdiction
Certify the question to a federal advisory committee

cards.explanation: Pullman abstention (Railroad Comm'n v. Pullman Co., 1941) applies when a federal-court decision on a federal constitutional question turns on an unclear state-law issue, and state-court interpretation might moot or alter the federal question. The federal court should abstain (often by staying proceedings) to allow state courts the first opportunity to clarify the state law, avoiding unnecessary federal constitutional adjudication.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Railroad Commission of Texas v. Pullman Co., 312 U.S. 496 (1941)
Harris County Comm'rs Court v. Moore, 420 U.S. 77 (1975)

cards.stem: A private plaintiff sues a state official in federal court seeking PROSPECTIVE injunctive relief to halt ongoing federal-law violations. Despite state sovereign immunity, the suit is most likely:

choices.text: Barred by the 11th Amendment
Permitted under the Ex parte Young exception
Permitted only with state consent
Barred unless Congress has abrogated sovereign immunity

cards.explanation: Ex parte Young (1908) permits federal-court suits against state officials in their official capacity for prospective injunctive relief to halt ongoing federal-law violations. The fiction is that the state official, when violating federal law, is not acting as the state and thus the 11A does not bar suit. The exception does not extend to retrospective monetary damages from the state treasury.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

cards.stem: A federal court is asked to enjoin enforcement of a state regulatory scheme involving complex state administrative procedures. The federal court should likely:

choices.text: Decide the merits without abstention
Abstain under Burford v. Sun Oil to avoid disrupting complex state regulatory schemes
Apply Pullman abstention
Dismiss for lack of jurisdiction

cards.explanation: Burford v. Sun Oil Co. (1943) established abstention where federal-court adjudication would disrupt state efforts to establish coherent policy through specialized regulatory schemes (e.g., oil and gas regulation, complex insurance regulation). Abstention is appropriate where federal review would interfere with state administrative process or generate inconsistent federal/state interpretations.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Burford v. Sun Oil Co., 319 U.S. 315 (1943)
New Orleans Public Service v. New Orleans, 491 U.S. 350 (1989)

cards.stem: Parallel state and federal litigation involves the same parties and claims. The federal court considers staying or dismissing the federal action in deference to the state proceeding. The appropriate analysis is:

choices.text: Automatic dismissal in deference to state court
Colorado River exceptional-circumstances test
Younger abstention only
Pullman abstention only

cards.explanation: Colorado River Water Conservation District v. United States (1976) established that a federal court may stay or dismiss a federal action in favor of parallel state-court litigation only in 'exceptional circumstances.' Factors include: which court first assumed jurisdiction, inconvenience of the federal forum, desirability of avoiding piecemeal litigation, order of jurisdiction, federal-law primacy, and adequacy of state proceedings.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Moses H. Cone Memorial Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1 (1983)

cards.stem: Congress applies federal labor standards (FLSA) to state employees. Per current Supreme Court doctrine, the application is:

choices.text: Unconstitutional under the 10th Amendment
Constitutional under the Commerce Clause
Constitutional only under the Spending Clause
Unconstitutional under National League of Cities

cards.explanation: Garcia v. San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority (1985) overruled National League of Cities v. Usery (1976) and held that federal labor laws apply to state and local governments. The Court held that the Tenth Amendment is not violated when Congress regulates state activities under valid Commerce Clause authority; states' interests are protected through the political process rather than judicial review.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Garcia v. San Antonio Metro. Transit Auth., 469 U.S. 528 (1985)
National League of Cities v. Usery, 426 U.S. 833 (1976)

cards.stem: Congress purports to authorize private suits against non-consenting states in STATE COURT for federal-law violations. Per Supreme Court doctrine, the authorization is:

choices.text: Constitutional under the Supremacy Clause
Unconstitutional — state sovereign immunity extends to state courts
Constitutional with the state's consent
Constitutional under the 14A § 5 enforcement power

cards.explanation: Alden v. Maine (1999) held that state sovereign immunity, founded on principles broader than the 11A, bars Congress from authorizing private suits against non-consenting states in STATE court for violations of federal law (here, the FLSA). The Court relied on structural principles of federalism and the dignity of state sovereignty.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Federal Maritime Commission v. South Carolina State Ports Authority, 535 U.S. 743 (2002)

cards.stem: A federal regulatory agency conducts administrative adjudication against a non-consenting state. Per Supreme Court doctrine, the proceeding is:

choices.text: Permitted as administrative, not judicial, action
Barred by state sovereign immunity
Permitted only if Congress has provided clear authorization
Permitted under the Necessary and Proper Clause

cards.explanation: Federal Maritime Commission v. South Carolina State Ports Authority (2002) extended state sovereign immunity to federal-agency adjudications that resemble lawsuits against the state. The Court held that the dignity-of-states principles underlying sovereign immunity are not avoided by relabeling adjudication as 'administrative.'
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Federal Maritime Commission v. South Carolina State Ports Authority, 535 U.S. 743 (2002)

cards.stem: Congress enacts a statute purporting to authorize private suits against states for damages, claiming this is necessary to enforce 14A rights. The state asserts sovereign immunity. Per Supreme Court doctrine, the statute must:

choices.text: Survive strict scrutiny
Be congruent and proportional to the constitutional violation it addresses
Be narrowly tailored to a compelling interest
Be authorized by the President

cards.explanation: City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) established that Congress's 14A § 5 enforcement power requires legislation to be 'congruent and proportional' to the constitutional violation it addresses. Congress can abrogate state sovereign immunity through § 5 legislation, but only where the legislative remedy fits the underlying constitutional injury (Kimel, Garrett, Lane, Coleman line of cases).
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997)

cards.stem: Congress enacts a statute providing that an executive action may be vetoed by a single house of Congress without presentment to the President. Per Supreme Court doctrine, the statute is:

choices.text: Constitutional as a permissible legislative oversight mechanism
Unconstitutional as violating bicameralism and presentment
Constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Constitutional only with the President's consent

cards.explanation: INS v. Chadha (1983) struck down the legislative veto. Congress may take legally binding action only through bicameralism (passage by both houses) and presentment (presentation to the President for signature or veto). Single-house or two-house actions affecting legal rights, without presentment, violate Article I § 7.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

citations.label: Clinton v. City of New York, 524 U.S. 417 (1998)

cards.stem: Congress enacts a statute giving the Comptroller General (an officer removable only by Congress through joint resolution) the authority to determine federal spending levels. Per Supreme Court doctrine, this is:

choices.text: Constitutional under Congress's spending power
Unconstitutional because the Comptroller General is performing executive functions while removable by Congress
Constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause
Constitutional under the Speech and Debate Clause

cards.explanation: Bowsher v. Synar (1986) struck down a portion of the Gramm-Rudman-Hollings Act that vested executive functions (determining mandatory spending cuts) in the Comptroller General, who is removable only by Congress. Congress cannot retain control over the execution of laws by giving executive functions to officers it can remove.
cards.attribution: Claude PR #3 (validated bank). Awaiting expert review.

cards.stem: Congress establishes the U.S. Sentencing Commission, an independent body within the judicial branch authorized to promulgate binding sentencing guidelines. The constitutionality is most likely:

choices.text: Unconstitutional because it grants legislative power to a non-legislative body
Constitutional under the non-delegation doctrine and inter-branch placement
Unconstitutional as commandeering of judicial officers
Subject to strict scrutiny

cards.explanation: Mistretta v. United States (1989) upheld the Sentencing Commission against non-delegation and separation-of-powers challenges. Congress may delegate rulemaking authority with sufficient guidance ('intelligible principle'), and placing a rulemaking body in the judicial branch with judicial members does not violate separation of powers as long as it does not interfere with judicial functions.
